name: dig
plain: `dig` asks the Domain Name System questions and shows the full answer. DNS is the phone book of the internet: it turns names such as example.com into IP addresses and holds other records (mail servers, text notes, name servers).
In security work dig is how you enumerate a domain: find mail servers, name servers, hidden subdomains, and test whether a name server leaks its whole zone (a zone transfer).
when: Find the IP address of a name (and the reverse).
List mail (MX), name (NS) and text (TXT) records.
Try a zone transfer on a lab DNS server.
Check which DNS server answers and how long it takes.
Trace how a name is resolved from the root.

examples.title: A simple lookup
examples.explain: Shows the question, the answer section (the A record, i.e. the IPv4 address) and some statistics.

examples.title: Just the answer
examples.explain: +short prints only the answer, one line per record: ideal for scripts.

examples.title: A specific record type
examples.cmd:
dig example.com MX
dig example.com TXT
dig example.com NS
examples.explain: MX is mail servers, TXT is free text (SPF, verification codes), NS lists the name servers.

examples.title: Ask a particular server
examples.explain: @server sends the question to that server instead of your default. Essential in labs with their own DNS.

examples.title: Reverse lookup
examples.explain: -x turns an IP back into a name (a PTR record).

examples.title: Everything the server will tell you
examples.explain: ANY asks for all record types, but many servers now refuse or answer partially.

examples.title: Zone transfer attempt
examples.explain: AXFR asks for a copy of the entire zone. A misconfigured server returns every host name: a classic CTF finding.

examples.title: Trace the resolution
examples.explain: Starts at the root servers and follows the delegation down to the answer.

examples.title: Clean output
examples.explain: +noall hides everything, +answer shows only the answer section.

examples.title: Over TCP
examples.explain: Forces TCP instead of UDP, useful if UDP is blocked or the answer is large.

options.plain: Name server to ask (name or IP).
Record type: A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME, SOA, PTR, SRV, ANY, AXFR.
Same as giving the type, written as an option.
Batch mode: read queries from a file.
Give the name as an option.
Ask the server not to / to look things up for you.
Show or hide the statistics and the command line.

mistakes: Asking your default resolver about a lab domain that only the lab DNS knows: use @server.
Forgetting that ANY is often refused: query each type.
Reading 'NOERROR' with no answer as success: the name exists but has no record of that type.
Trying a zone transfer on servers you are not authorised to test.
Mixing up the question section with the answer section.
try: Look up the A, MX, NS and TXT records of a domain you own.
Run dig +trace on a name and count the steps.
Try dig axfr against a deliberately vulnerable lab DNS.
see_also: nslookup(1), host(1), whois(1), nmap(1) (dns-* scripts), dnsrecon, fierce, gobuster(1) (dns mode).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
